slides.notes: A light day of definition and context: what we are doing and why. Brian takes a full class period; you can also fold it into another lesson. Goals: students understand the purpose of YAWP!, read a sample essay, and create their YAWP! accounts. Have the sample essay (“Bored in the USA,” or your own) printed or shared, and your class’s join link ready.

runs.text: I have a twin who is a blonde-haired version of me.
I met my wife in high school.

slides.notes: These are Brian’s own slides, left as an example. Make your own the same way: three statements about you, two true and one believable lie, and a photo or two that make you human (self-deprecating works best). Or delete these slides and play the game without them. How Brian plays it: let students ask questions and "vibe it out," take guesses, then a vote by show of hands for each one. The reveal: he was not born in Canada.

runs.text: I’m here because I love writing and helping other people become better writers.

slides.notes: These are Brian’s own slides, left as an example. Make your own the same way: three statements about you, two true and one believable lie, and a photo or two that make you human (self-deprecating works best). Or delete these slides and play the game without them. Brian’s line: "Here’s my blonde-haired, blue-eyed twin brother Patrick and me, on our first day of kindergarten at a school that made us wear these uniforms. I’m obviously the handsome fella on the left."

elements.alt: A photo of Brian from the 1990s.

slides.notes: These are Brian’s own slides, left as an example. Make your own the same way: three statements about you, two true and one believable lie, and a photo or two that make you human (self-deprecating works best). Or delete these slides and play the game without them. Brian’s line: "A short 12 or 13 years later, I looked like this. My wife and I did in fact meet in high school; this is us in our freshman year of college."

runs.text: Write your own. Remember, the truths have to be true, and
the lie has to be believable!

slides.notes: Students write three statements at their desks. Keep the lies believable ("I have eight children" or "I can fly" won’t work). Then share with a neighbor or table and guess. Watch the room come to life. Invite a few to try to stump the whole class, or you. The point is to disarm the room and have fun together at the top of the program.

runs.text: I sound my barbaric yawp over the roofs of the world.

slides.notes: Ask what they think "yawp" means. A yell, a sound, a scream from a rooftop: all good. Say "yes, and" to every answer; how you respond matters to the whole room, not just the student who spoke. Then Brian’s framing: your yawp is your voice. Imagine everything inside you, your thoughts, opinions, experiences, relationships, the music in your head, and give it all one big, mighty sound. That is your yawp, and it is unique to you. In this program we unleash it through writing.

runs.text: Because writing is one of the most effective ways of
(What other ways can we express ourselves?)

slides.notes: Lead a quick discussion. How might a happy person express it without words? (Smile, laugh.) An angry one? Then: writing articulates something for yourself and others, and it lasts. That permanence is why writing is power. Most students hear this and think, "I want some of that." Day 1 is about getting them to buy in.

Use "Bored in the USA" (the Sample essay handout, next to this deck in the Modules), or your own sample, as long as it follows our form (intro ending in a thesis, body paragraphs, conclusion). Everyone has a copy. Before reading, ask everyone to underline or highlight anything interesting, at least one thing per paragraph. Volunteers read aloud, a paragraph each. Don’t overanalyze.

runs.text: What do you like about this essay?
Do you agree with the writer?

slides.notes: Keep it simple: "Tell me one thing you underlined and why." The point is that they’re talking. The question you must land is the third: the main point is the thesis statement, the last sentence of the introduction. Have everyone underline it. It’s one sentence that captures the main argument of the whole essay, and you’ll come back to it for weeks.

elements.alt: The critical essay form: introduction, body paragraphs and conclusion.

slides.notes: The shape of the essay they just read and the one they are about to write. Point at the thesis: the most important part, the last sentence of the intro. Don’t spend long here; it’s also a handout, and you’ll come back to it.

runs.text: Over the course of our sessions, you will learn how to write a
like the one we just read. To accomplish this, we will:
Analyze and discuss our opinions about the topic

slides.notes: You can tell them the topic is coming later. This is a writing class: they’ll spend real time writing and thinking about what they think.

, or put the QR code up on the board
Students open it on their device and create an account

elements.alt: The class's join link and QR code on the Students tab.

slides.notes: The current sign-up flow. Each class has its own join link and QR code on its Students tab. The class code shown there is for your reference only; it is not enough to join. Students pick a display name, a handle and a password. Keep a note of handles and passwords, or give the class a pattern to follow, to avoid the inevitable forgotten passwords; you can reset a student’s password from the Students tab.

elements.alt: The YAWP! "Create your student account" page.

runs.text: Open the link or scan the QR code

slides.notes: Walk the room while students sign up. Handles are 3 to 30 characters: letters, numbers, dots, underscores and hyphens. Already have an account? They can log in from the same page.

elements.alt: The YAWP! student dashboard after joining.

runs.text: Your class is on your dashboard
Open it to see your assignments
Start an assignment to open your document

slides.notes: Once they’re in, have them open the class and start the first assignment you’ve given them, which creates their document. Next class they open the same document (not a new one) and begin pre-writing.
Before students leave, make sure everyone has joined your class and started the assignment. Collect any forgotten handles now; it saves time next class.
